questions.prompt: What does electric current measure?
options: Number of neutrons in a cell.
questions.explanation: Current is charge transferred per time: I = Q/t. Its unit is the ampere, A.

questions.prompt: What does a current of 1 A mean?
options: 1 J is stored in every electron.
1 C passes a point each second.
1 Ω passes a point each second.
1 V is used up every second.
questions.explanation: One ampere is one coulomb per second: 1 A = 1 C/s.

questions.prompt: What does closing a switch do in a simple battery loop?
questions.explanation: A complete loop permits sustained current. Mobile charges were present throughout the metal before closure.

questions.prompt: In a steady series circuit, how does current before a resistor compare with current after it?
options: The current after is always zero.
The current before is twice the current after.
The resistor creates extra charge, so current after is greater.
questions.explanation: Charge does not accumulate indefinitely in a steady series loop. Energy transfers, while the same charge rate continues.

questions.prompt: 6 C passes a point in 3 s. What is the current?
questions.explanation: I = Q/t = 6 C ÷ 3 s = 2 C/s = 2 A.

questions.prompt: A steady current is 0.5 A for 8 s. How much charge passes?
questions.explanation: Q = It = 0.5 A × 8 s = 4 C. The circuit does not use up this charge.

questions.prompt: Which direction is conventional current in the external circuit?
options: From negative towards positive by definition.
Only from Earth to a lamp.
Only towards the cell’s centre from both sides.
questions.explanation: Conventional current follows positive-charge flow. Metal electrons drift in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Which carriers drift through ordinary metal wires?
options: Positive ion cores flowing freely around the loop.
questions.explanation: Mobile electrons carry the net drift current; positive ion cores remain in the lattice.

questions.prompt: At a junction, 0.7 A arrives and one branch takes 0.2 A. What current takes the other branch?
questions.explanation: In a steady junction, entering current equals leaving current. The remaining branch current is 0.7 − 0.2 = 0.5 A.

questions.prompt: Why can a lamp respond quickly when electrons drift slowly?
options: One electron must complete the whole loop before the lamp responds.
An electrical signal propagates through a circuit with charges already present.
The lamp creates electrons from light first.
Electrons drift at the speed of light in every metal.
questions.explanation: Individual drift and electrical signal propagation are different. The current involves mobile charges already present around the circuit.

questions.prompt: What is potential difference?
options: Energy transferred per unit charge between two points.
The number of electrons stored in a wire.
questions.explanation: V = E/Q. Voltage compares two points and is measured in joules per coulomb, or volts.

questions.prompt: What does 1 V mean?
questions.explanation: The volt is a joule per coulomb: 1 V = 1 J/C. It is not itself a flow rate.

questions.prompt: In the pizza model, what does the shop represent?
questions.explanation: The shop supplies pizzas as the cell supplies energy per charge. Couriers represent charge packets.

questions.prompt: In the pizza model, what happens to couriers after the party?
options: They are destroyed as the lamp uses charge.
They return to the shop without the delivered energy badge.
They remain permanently at the party.
questions.explanation: Energy transfers at the component; charge continues around a complete loop.

questions.prompt: A component transfers 12 J when 2 C passes. What is its potential difference?
Across a 3 V component, 4 C passes. How much energy transfers?
questions.explanation: E = VQ = 3 V × 4 C = 12 J.

questions.prompt: Why is voltage not the same thing as current?
options: Voltage is energy per charge; current is charge per time.
Both mean charge per time in different colours.
Voltage counts only protons and current only neutrons.
Voltage is always zero when current is non-zero.
questions.explanation: Potential difference and charge-flow rate are distinct physical quantities with different units.

questions.prompt: In a two-resistor series network, the supply is 6 V and one resistor has 2 V. What is the other potential difference?
questions.explanation: Series potential differences add to the supply voltage, neglecting wire and internal resistance: 6 − 2 = 4 V.

questions.prompt: At fixed 3 Ω resistance, the supply changes from 3 V to 6 V. How do current and energy per coulomb change?
options: Only energy per coulomb doubles; current is unchanged.
Current halves while energy per coulomb doubles.
questions.explanation: I = V/R doubles when V doubles at fixed R. Energy per coulomb is V and doubles too.

questions.prompt: What is an important limit of the pizza model?
options: There is no complete path in any real circuit.
Real circuit energy transfer involves electromagnetic fields, not literal parcels carried on electrons.
questions.explanation: The analogy separates charge circulation from energy transfer. It does not describe the full electromagnetic mechanism.

questions.prompt: What unit measures resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms. A, C and W measure current, charge and power respectively.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives current from voltage and resistance?
questions.explanation: Rearrange V = IR by dividing both sides by R. Use volts and ohms to obtain amps.

questions.prompt: For an ohmic resistor, when does current stay proportional to voltage?
options: Only when its charge is used up.
When temperature and other physical conditions stay constant.
Only when it is an insulator with zero current.
questions.explanation: Ohm’s law describes a constant-resistance relationship under unchanged physical conditions.

questions.prompt: At fixed voltage, what happens when resistance increases?
options: Current stays identical in every circuit.
questions.explanation: I = V/R. Increasing the denominator at fixed V reduces the steady current.

questions.prompt: A 20 Ω resistor has 6 V across it. What current flows?
A resistor has 4 V across it and 0.20 A through it. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation: R = V/I = 4/0.20 = 20 Ω. Divide by 0.20, rather than multiply.

questions.prompt: At fixed resistance, what does doubling voltage do to current?
options: Makes it four times as large.
questions.explanation: Direct proportion means the same multiplicative change in V and I when R is constant.

questions.prompt: Why can an incandescent filament lamp have a curved I–V graph?
options: It uses up more electrons at higher voltage.
Every conductor must have a straight I–V graph.
Its temperature and resistance rise as current heats it.
questions.explanation: Heating changes the filament’s resistance, so it is not a constant-temperature ohmic resistor across its full range.

questions.prompt: Why does R = V/I at one operating point not prove Ohm’s law?
options: Many components have a ratio at one point without a constant ratio across voltages.
The ratio cannot ever be calculated.
Ohm’s law requires current to decrease when voltage increases.
questions.explanation: An ohmic test checks proportionality over several readings with temperature and conditions controlled.

questions.prompt: Why should R not be obtained from 0 V divided by 0 A?
options: Every resistor has zero resistance at zero voltage.
0/0 is undefined; use a non-zero point or the line gradient.
Zero current proves infinite resistance for every component.
The meter always measures protons at zero voltage.
questions.explanation: The ratio at the origin is indeterminate. A constant-resistance line’s non-zero points or gradient provide the resistance.

questions.prompt: How should an ammeter be connected?
options: Directly across the supply without a load.
In place of both supply terminals at once.
In series with the measured path.
Outside the circuit with no connection.
questions.explanation: An ammeter measures current through a path. Its very low resistance makes a direct supply connection inappropriate.

questions.prompt: How should a voltmeter be connected?
options: Only in series as the sole path.
In parallel across the component or network.
questions.explanation: A voltmeter compares two points across the measured component and has high resistance.

questions.prompt: On our I–V graph, what is on the horizontal axis?
questions.explanation: Our graph plots I vertically against V horizontally. Axis orientation matters when interpreting gradient.

questions.prompt: What graph represents an ohmic resistor at constant temperature?
options: A horizontal line at non-zero current for all voltages.
A straight I–V line through the origin.
A circle centred on the origin.
An arbitrary curve whose slope changes continuously.
questions.explanation: Direct proportion means a straight line through (0,0) for I versus V.

questions.prompt: For I vertically and V horizontally, what does the gradient equal?
questions.explanation: Gradient is ΔI/ΔV. Since I = V/R, it equals reciprocal resistance, in A/V.

questions.prompt: Which I–V line means a lower resistance under these axis conventions?
options: Any line with a higher maximum x-axis label.
questions.explanation: At a given voltage, lower resistance permits greater current, so I/V and the graph gradient are larger.

questions.prompt: Why should one I–V dataset keep the same resistor and temperature?
options: To test voltage–current proportionality for fixed physical conditions.
To make charge disappear at the same rate.
Because voltage is not allowed to change.
questions.explanation: Changing resistor or temperature changes resistance and creates a different relationship, not another point on the same controlled test.

questions.prompt: If V is plotted vertically against I horizontally, what is the ohmic gradient?
questions.explanation: With V = RI, the gradient ΔV/ΔI equals resistance. Always read the axis labels before interpreting slope.

questions.prompt: A graph rises 0.20 A over a 4 V horizontal change. What resistance does it indicate?
questions.explanation: The I–V gradient is 0.20/4 = 0.05 A/V = 1/R, so R = 1/0.05 = 20 Ω.

questions.prompt: Why does our ideal voltmeter not materially change branch current?
options: It has zero resistance and short-circuits the branch.
It creates exactly the same charge it uses.
It connects to only one point.
It is modelled with infinite resistance and draws no current.
questions.explanation: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance. Real voltmeters have high, finite resistance, which can affect sensitive circuits.

questions.prompt: What describes two resistors in series?
options: They are in one path, one after the other.
They are connected across the same two junctions.
Neither is connected to the supply.
questions.explanation: Series means a single sequential path, so steady current is the same through both components.

questions.prompt: What describes two resistors in parallel?
options: They always carry exactly equal currents.
They connect across the same two junctions.
Their resistances must be added directly.
Only one can be connected at a time.
questions.explanation: Parallel branches share the same potential difference; their currents depend on their resistances.

questions.prompt: What is the total resistance of 20 Ω and 40 Ω in series?
questions.explanation: For series resistors, R_total = R₁ + R₂ = 20 + 40 = 60 Ω.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is the same across ideal parallel branches?
options: Number of components in each branch.
questions.explanation: Each branch connects across the same pair of junctions and therefore has the same voltage.

questions.prompt: A 6 V supply drives 20 Ω and 40 Ω in series. What is the current?
questions.explanation: The total resistance is 60 Ω, so I = 6/60 = 0.10 A through both resistors.

questions.prompt: At 6 V, how much current flows in a 40 Ω parallel branch?
questions.explanation: That branch has the full 6 V, so I₂ = 6/40 = 0.15 A.

questions.prompt: At 6 V, 20 Ω and 40 Ω are in parallel. What is supply current?
questions.explanation: Branch currents are 6/20 = 0.30 A and 6/40 = 0.15 A. Their sum is 0.45 A.

questions.prompt: What happens to equivalent resistance when an extra finite-resistance parallel branch is added?
options: It is unchanged for every new branch.
It becomes the sum of all branch resistances.
questions.explanation: The extra branch provides another conducting path. For positive branch resistances, equivalent resistance is lower than before.

questions.prompt: For 20 Ω and 40 Ω in parallel, which total resistance is correct?
questions.explanation: R_total = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 800/60 ≈ 13.33 Ω, less than either branch resistance.

questions.prompt: In a series circuit, current is 0.10 A through 20 Ω and 40 Ω. What are the voltage drops?
questions.explanation: V₁ = IR₁ = 0.10 × 20 = 2 V; V₂ = 0.10 × 40 = 4 V. The larger resistance takes the larger share of voltage.

questions.prompt: Which wire factor describes the material itself at a stated temperature?
questions.explanation: Resistivity is a material property in Ω m. Resistance also depends on geometry: R = ρL/A.

questions.prompt: Keeping material, area and temperature fixed, what does doubling wire length do?
questions.explanation: R is directly proportional to L for a uniform wire at fixed resistivity and area.

questions.prompt: Keeping other factors fixed, what does increasing wire cross-sectional area do?
options: Changes all electrons to positive particles.
questions.explanation: R = ρL/A. A larger conducting area provides more parallel paths and lowers resistance.

questions.prompt: What is electrical power?
questions.explanation: P = E/t, measured in watts, where 1 W = 1 J/s. For a circuit component, P = VI.

questions.prompt: A 6 V component carries 0.30 A. What is its power?
A component transfers energy at 2 W for 10 s. How much energy transfers?
For our ordinary metal models, what usually happens when temperature increases?
options: Resistance increases because lattice vibrations increase scattering.
Positive ion cores flow around the loop.
Every material has an identical temperature response.
questions.explanation: These approximate metal models have positive temperature coefficients. Other materials and temperature ranges can behave differently.

questions.prompt: Keeping material, length and temperature fixed, what does doubling a round wire’s diameter do to resistance?
questions.explanation: Area A = π(d/2)² grows by a factor of four, so R = ρL/A falls to one quarter.

questions.prompt: At fixed transmitted power, why can higher transmission voltage reduce cable losses?
options: Voltage itself makes the cable’s resistivity zero.
It removes the need for a complete circuit.
It allows lower current, reducing I²R heating without needing a change in cable resistance.
It makes current and power identical quantities.
questions.explanation: P = VI, so higher V permits lower I at the same P. Cable heating depends on I²R; the resistance need not decrease.

questions.prompt: At fixed supply voltage, what happens to resistor power if resistance doubles?
questions.explanation: At fixed V, P = V²/R, so doubling R halves total power. The statement P = I²R must be used with the actual changed current, not a falsely fixed I.
